lessons.title: Linear search
lessons.summary: Checking every item, one by one, until you find the target.
lessons.notes:
A **linear search** checks a list item by item, from the very start, until it finds the target — or reaches the end without finding it.

```python
target = input()
found = False
for item in items:
    if item == target:
        found = True
print(found)
```

It's called "linear" because the number of checks needed grows in a straight line with the size of the list — search a list of 1,000 items, and in the worst case you check all 1,000.

---

**Best case**: the target is the very first item — just 1 check.
**Worst case**: the target is the last item, or isn't in the list at all — every single item gets checked.

Linear search works on **any** list, sorted or not — that's its one real advantage over binary search, which only works on a sorted list (next lesson).
lessons.worked_example:
count = int(input())
names = [input() for _ in range(count)]
target = input()
found = False
for name in names:
    if name == target:
        found = True
print("Found" if found else "Not found")
lessons.worked_example_note: found starts False and only flips to True if a matching item turns up during the loop - if the loop finishes without a match, it stays False.

lessons.title: Linear search: tracing and efficiency
lessons.summary: How many checks it really takes, and how to trace one step by step.
lessons.notes:
Linear search's efficiency depends entirely on **where** the target is:

| List size | Best case (first item) | Worst case (last item / not found) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 10 items | 1 check | 10 checks |
| 1,000 items | 1 check | 1,000 checks |
| 1,000,000 items | 1 check | 1,000,000 checks |

On average, you'd expect to check about **half** the list before finding a random target. This straight-line relationship between list size and worst-case checks is why linear search is described as having **linear time complexity** — double the list, and (in the worst case) you double the work.

---

**Tracing a linear search.** Exam questions often ask you to trace through a search step by step, listing each item checked:

```text
List: [12, 45, 7, 23, 56]
Target: 23

Check index 0: 12 - no match
Check index 1: 45 - no match
Check index 2: 7 - no match
Check index 3: 23 - match! Stop.
```

Notice the search **stops immediately** once it finds a match — it never checks index 4, even though there's still an item there.
lessons.worked_example:
n = int(input())
items = [int(input()) for _ in range(n)]
target = int(input())
for i in range(len(items)):
    print(f"Check index {i}: {items[i]}")
    if items[i] == target:
        break
lessons.worked_example_note: break stops the loop the instant a match is found, which is why the trace doesn't include every index - only the ones actually checked before stopping.

lessons.title: Binary search
lessons.summary: A much faster search - but only on a list that's already sorted.
lessons.notes:
**Binary search** is a much faster way to search — but it only works on a list that's already **sorted**.

How it works: check the middle item.
- If it's the target, done.
- If the target is smaller, it must be in the left half — search there next.
- If the target is bigger, it must be in the right half — search there next.
- Repeat, each time on a half the size of before, until found or there's nothing left to search.

```python
low = 0
high = len(items) - 1
while low <= high:
    mid = (low + high) // 2
    if items[mid] == target:
        # found it at index mid
        break
    elif items[mid] < target:
        low = mid + 1
    else:
        high = mid - 1
```

---

**Why it's faster.** Each check throws away half of what's left to search — like the "guess a number 1-100" game, where guessing the middle each time finds any number in at most 7 guesses, not 100. A binary search of 1,000,000 items takes at most about 20 checks, compared to up to 1,000,000 for linear search.
lessons.worked_example:
n = int(input())
items = [int(input()) for _ in range(n)]
target = int(input())
low = 0
high = n - 1
result = -1
while low <= high:
    mid = (low + high) // 2
    if items[mid] == target:
        result = mid
        break
    elif items[mid] < target:
        low = mid + 1
    else:
        high = mid - 1
print(result)
lessons.worked_example_note: low and high mark the edges of the section still worth searching - every time round the loop, mid either matches, or one of low/high moves past mid, shrinking that section by half.

lessons.title: Bubble sort and insertion sort
lessons.summary: Two simple ways to sort a list, by swapping neighbours or by building up a sorted section.
lessons.notes:
Two simple ways to sort a list, both worth knowing for OCR.

**Bubble sort** repeatedly steps through the list, comparing each pair of neighbours and swapping them if they're in the wrong order. Each full pass "bubbles" the largest unsorted value up to its correct position at the end. Keep making passes until a whole pass makes no swaps — the list is sorted.

```text
[5, 2, 8, 1]
Pass 1: compare 5,2 -> swap -> [2, 5, 8, 1]
        compare 5,8 -> no swap -> [2, 5, 8, 1]
        compare 8,1 -> swap -> [2, 5, 1, 8]
Pass 2: compare 2,5 -> no swap
        compare 5,1 -> swap -> [2, 1, 5, 8]
        compare 5,8 -> no swap
Pass 3: compare 2,1 -> swap -> [1, 2, 5, 8]
        compare 2,5 -> no swap
        compare 5,8 -> no swap
Pass 4: no swaps at all -> sorted!
```

---

**Insertion sort** builds up a sorted section at the start of the list, one item at a time — take the next unsorted item, and slide it left into its correct place among the already-sorted items before it.

```text
[5, 2, 8, 1]
Start: [5] is trivially "sorted"
Insert 2: slides left past 5 -> [2, 5, 8, 1]
Insert 8: already bigger than 5, stays put -> [2, 5, 8, 1]
Insert 1: slides left past 8, 5, and 2 -> [1, 2, 5, 8]
```

Both end up sorted, but they get there differently — bubble sort repeatedly swaps neighbours across the *whole* list; insertion sort grows a sorted section from the *front*, one item at a time.
lessons.worked_example_note: Each pass (the outer loop) needs one fewer comparison than the last, since the biggest remaining value has already bubbled into place at the end.

lessons.title: Merge sort
lessons.summary: Divide the list down to single items, then merge them back together in order.
lessons.notes:
**Merge sort** takes a different approach: divide and conquer.

1. **Divide**: split the list in half, then split each half in half, and so on, until every "list" is just a single item (a single item is always already "sorted").
2. **Conquer (merge)**: merge pairs of sorted lists back together into bigger sorted lists, comparing their front items and taking the smaller each time, until it's all back into one fully sorted list.

```text
[5, 2, 8, 1]

Divide:
[5, 2, 8, 1] -> [5, 2] and [8, 1]
[5, 2] -> [5] and [2]
[8, 1] -> [8] and [1]

Merge:
[5] and [2] -> [2, 5]
[8] and [1] -> [1, 8]
[2, 5] and [1, 8] -> [1, 2, 5, 8]
```

---

**The merge step is the key skill.** Given two lists that are already sorted, merging them is simple: compare the front of each list, take the smaller one, and repeat until both lists are empty.

```python
def merge(left, right):
    result = []
    i = j = 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:
            result.append(left[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            result.append(right[j])
            j += 1
    result.extend(left[i:])
    result.extend(right[j:])
    return result
```

Merge sort is one of the trickier algorithms to write from scratch — for GCSE, the important thing is being able to **trace** it (show how a list gets split and merged back together) and understand *why* it works, more than writing the full recursive version unaided.
lessons.worked_example:
def merge(left, right):
    result = []
    i = j = 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:
            result.append(left[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            result.append(right[j])
            j += 1
    result.extend(left[i:])
    result.extend(right[j:])
    return result

n1 = int(input())
left = [int(input()) for _ in range(n1)]
n2 = int(input())
right = [int(input()) for _ in range(n2)]
print(" ".join(str(x) for x in merge(left, right)))
lessons.worked_example_note: i and j track how far into each list you've already taken from - whichever list's front item is smaller gets taken next, and its pointer moves on one.

quiz.question: What does a linear search do?
options: Checks each item in turn from the start until it finds the target or reaches the end
Jumps straight to the middle of the list
Only works on lists that are already sorted
Sorts the list first, then searches it
quiz.answer: Checks each item in turn from the start until it finds the target or reaches the end
quiz.explanation: Linear search works through a list one item at a time, in order, stopping as soon as it finds a match.

quiz.question: What is linear search's one real advantage over binary search?
options: It works on any list, sorted or not
It's always faster
It uses less memory
It never has a worst case
quiz.answer: It works on any list, sorted or not
quiz.explanation: Binary search needs a sorted list to work at all - linear search doesn't care about order.

quiz.question: In the worst case, how many items does a linear search of a 500-item list check?
options: It depends on the computer
quiz.explanation: The worst case is the target being last, or not present at all - either way, every one of the 500 items gets checked.

quiz.question: On average, about how many items does a linear search check before finding a random target?
options: About half the list
Always just 1
Always the whole list
It's impossible to say
quiz.explanation: Averaged across every possible position the target could be in, roughly half the list gets checked before a match turns up.

quiz.question: Why is linear search described as having "linear" time complexity?
options: Because the worst-case number of checks grows in a straight line with the list size
Because it only works on numbers
Because it uses a for loop
Because it's the fastest possible algorithm
quiz.answer: Because the worst-case number of checks grows in a straight line with the list size
quiz.explanation: Double the list size, and (in the worst case) you double the number of checks needed - a straight-line relationship.

quiz.question: During a trace of linear search, why does it stop checking as soon as a match is found?
options: There's no need to keep checking once the target has been located
Python forces every loop to stop after a match
It's a rule that only applies to sorted lists
It doesn't - it always checks every item regardless
quiz.answer: There's no need to keep checking once the target has been located
quiz.explanation: Once the target is found, checking further items would be wasted work, so the search (and the trace) stops there.

quiz.question: What must be true about a list before you can binary search it?
options: It must already be sorted
It must contain only numbers
It must have an even number of items
Nothing - it works on any list
quiz.explanation: Binary search relies on comparing the middle item to decide which half the target is in - that only works if the list is in order.

quiz.question: Each check in a binary search eliminates what fraction of the remaining list?
options: Half
A tenth
Just one item
It depends on the list's values
quiz.explanation: Whichever half the target isn't in gets discarded entirely, so the section still being searched halves every time.

quiz.question: Binary searching a sorted list of 1,000,000 items takes at most roughly how many checks?
options: About 20
Exactly 1
quiz.explanation: Because each check halves the list, you only need about log2(1,000,000) ≈ 20 checks in the worst case - dramatically fewer than linear search.

quiz.question: What does one pass of bubble sort do?
options: Compares each pair of neighbouring items, swapping them if they're in the wrong order
Picks the smallest item and moves it straight to the front
Splits the list in half
Checks if the list is already sorted, then stops immediately
quiz.answer: Compares each pair of neighbouring items, swapping them if they're in the wrong order
quiz.explanation: A single pass steps through the list comparing and swapping adjacent items - it takes several passes to fully sort the list.

quiz.question: How does bubble sort know the list is fully sorted and it can stop?
options: A whole pass goes by with no swaps at all
It counts exactly n passes and always stops there
The first item becomes the smallest in the list
It never stops on its own
quiz.answer: A whole pass goes by with no swaps at all
quiz.explanation: If a complete pass makes zero swaps, every neighbouring pair must already be in the right order, so the list is sorted.

quiz.question: What's the key difference between how bubble sort and insertion sort work?
options: Bubble sort repeatedly swaps neighbours across the whole list; insertion sort grows a sorted section from the front
They are exactly the same algorithm with different names
Insertion sort only works on lists of numbers
Bubble sort only works on lists that are already sorted
quiz.answer: Bubble sort repeatedly swaps neighbours across the whole list; insertion sort grows a sorted section from the front
quiz.explanation: Both end up sorted, but bubble sort compares/swaps pairs across the whole list each pass, while insertion sort builds up a sorted front section one item at a time.

quiz.question: What are the two stages of merge sort?
options: Divide the list down to single items, then merge them back together in sorted order
Compare every possible pair of items once
Pick the middle item and search left or right of it
Swap neighbouring items repeatedly until sorted
quiz.answer: Divide the list down to single items, then merge them back together in sorted order
quiz.explanation: Merge sort is "divide and conquer": split the list all the way down to single items, then merge pairs back together, largest merge last.

quiz.question: When merging two already-sorted lists together, how do you decide which item to take next?
options: Compare the front item of each list and take the smaller one
Always take from the first list until it's completely empty
Take items in whatever order they were originally in
Pick one at random
quiz.answer: Compare the front item of each list and take the smaller one
quiz.explanation: Since both lists are already sorted, the smaller of their two front items must be the next-smallest value overall.

quiz.question: Why might merge sort be considered harder to write from scratch than bubble or insertion sort?
options: It needs a way to keep dividing the list and then correctly merging the results back together
It doesn't actually sort the list at all
It only works on lists that are already sorted
It requires binary search to run first
quiz.answer: It needs a way to keep dividing the list and then correctly merging the results back together
quiz.explanation: Bubble and insertion sort are single loops over the list - merge sort needs both a splitting step and a merging step working together correctly.

tasks.title: Is it in the list?

hints: Loop through the values one at a time, checking each against the target as you go.
found = False; for v in values: if v == target: found = True — then print("Yes" if found else "No").

tasks.title: Find the position
tasks.brief: Input a whole number N, then N items of text, then a target to search for. Using a linear search, print the target's position (0-based), or `-1` if it isn't in the list.
hints: Stop as soon as you find a match, and remember the index it was found at.
for i in range(n): if values[i] == target: pos = i; break — starting pos at -1 before the loop.

tasks.title: Count the comparisons
tasks.brief: Input a whole number N, then N more whole numbers, then a target. Using a linear search, count how many items are actually checked before the search stops (whether it finds the target or reaches the end), and print that count.
hints: Increase the count on every check, including the one that finds the match, then stop straight away.
count = 0; for v in values: count += 1; if v == target: break — then print(count).

tasks.title: First match only
tasks.brief: Input a whole number N, then N more whole numbers, which may include duplicates, then a target. Using a linear search, print the position (0-based) of the **first** occurrence of the target in the list.
hints: A linear search naturally finds the first match, since it stops the instant it hits one.
for i in range(n): if values[i] == target: pos = i; break.

tasks.title: Trace the checks

for i in range(n): print(f"Check index {i}: {values[i]}"); if values[i] == target: break.

hints: Check the special cases (first item, last item, not present) before falling back to "Neither".
if target == values[0]: ... elif target == values[-1]: ... elif target not in values: ... else: print("Neither").

tasks.title: Count all occurrences
tasks.brief: Input a whole number N, then N more whole numbers, which may include duplicates, then a target. Print how many times the target appears in the list in total — this time checking every item, not stopping at the first match.

tasks.title: Case-insensitive name search

if values[i].lower() == target.lower(): pos = i; break.

tasks.title: Binary search - find the position

tasks.title: Bubble sort
tasks.brief: Input a whole number N, then N more whole numbers. Sort them using bubble sort, and print the sorted list, all on one line separated by spaces.
hints: A pair of nested loops: the outer one for each pass, the inner one comparing and swapping neighbours.
for i in range(n): for j in range(n - 1 - i): if values[j] > values[j + 1]: values[j], values[j + 1] = values[j + 1], values[j].

tasks.title: Count the swaps

hints: Add one to a counter every time two neighbours actually get swapped.
swaps = 0; ... if values[j] > values[j + 1]: values[j], values[j + 1] = values[j + 1], values[j]; swaps += 1.

tasks.title: Insertion sort
tasks.brief: Input a whole number N, then N more whole numbers. Sort them using insertion sort, and print the sorted list, all on one line separated by spaces.
hints: Starting from the second item, slide each one left past any larger items already in the sorted section before it.
for i in range(1, n): key = values[i]; j = i - 1; while j >= 0 and values[j] > key: values[j + 1] = values[j]; j -= 1; values[j + 1] = key.

tasks.title: Trace an insertion sort

hints: Print the whole list once per pass of the outer loop, after that pass's insertion is finished.
for i in range(1, n): ...(insert values[i] into place)...; print(" ".join(str(x) for x in values)).

tasks.title: Merge two sorted lists
